    Huron · Implementation atlas

    Security: Authorization

    Principals, bindings, scopes, and the deny-by-default decision that stands between every authenticated actor and Huron's catalog.

    Security ownerDeny-by-default decisions12 UML viewsOffline-ready

    Implementation snapshot: 16 September 2026, working tree based on e71e685. The editable Markdown source contains all Mermaid diagrams and responsibility notes.

    RBAC gives Huron its deny-by-default authorization: a pure decision engine over principals, bindings, and scopes in core.security.rules; a closed role vocabulary that compiles to those bindings; classification-aware discovery; an actor-bound AccessPolicy in core.security that authorized operations consult; governance workflows that grant roles, define policies, and administer service accounts; and PostgreSQL and in-memory stores that persist the grants.

    This is one class model presented in focused views. It includes every class, protocol, enum, and dataclass retained in Security's rules.py and roles.py, its colocated authorization and governance workflows, consumer-owned fact/store protocols, and the two Metastore RBAC adapters at their public surface. Security also owns governance records. Catalog's hierarchy values, the authentication resolvers that produce the actor, and the API route handlers are neighbors shown only where they collaborate; the catalog atlas and the authentication design cover their internals. Module-level functions are drawn as <<Module>> boxes so that the decision procedure, which is a function rather than a class, still appears in the model. Methods show the public operations and important types, with long parameter lists abbreviated. This is a Python class diagram, not a database ER diagram or an exhaustive signature reference.

    Authentication and RBAC are two views of one Security owner. Security imports Foundation only, never Catalog or adapters. CatalogFacts projects just the authoritative facts it needs. Root exports publish workflow construction; _impl links are source navigation, not supported imports. Migration verification is recorded in the roadmap.

    Currency matters: the RBAC design describes intent that the inspected source does not yet implement, including raw payload read as a stricter capability, classification clearance on stored bindings, DENY bindings written through the API, API-key scope narrowing, and the planned P3 integrity authority. Section 12 lists each gap. A capability name in the vocabulary proves only that a role may carry it; the enforcement table in section 6 says where it is checked.

    Reading the diagrams

    • A --> B: association/reference, including ID-based domain relationships.
    • A ..> B: uses, creates, or returns B; the label states which.
    • A *-- B: A contains B as part of its object structure.
    • A --|> B: actual Python inheritance.
    • A ..|> B: structural conformance to a Python protocol, not inheritance.
    • <<Protocol>>, <<Frozen>>, <<Enum>>, <<Module>>, <<External>>, and <<Neighbor>> identify roles. <<Module>> boxes list module-level functions and constants; a $ suffix marks a classmethod or class-level constant.
    • Frozen dataclasses prevent field reassignment. The governance records (RoleBindingRecord, ServiceAccount, Policy, PolicyAttachment) are slotted but not frozen.
    • Identifier strings follow Principal.identifiers: user:{subject}, sa:{subject}, group:{name}. Bindings address one identifier string; the engine never compares principal objects.

    1. RBAC at a glance

    The overview follows one request: authentication produces a Principal; the AccessPolicy bound to that actor loads current bindings, resolves the target resource's scope with its ancestry, and asks the pure engine for a decision. Roles never reach the engine; they are compiled to plain capability bindings when a grant is stored and reconstructed from rows when bindings are read. Discovery is a separate computation over the same bindings that also consults the classification vocabulary.

    Responsibility Owner Important contract
    Decide a capability question decide() in core.security.rules Deny by default. Consider only bindings that match the principal, cover the scope, are unexpired, and name the capability. Any DENY wins; otherwise the first ALLOW at dataset, project, organization, or system level whose layer restriction admits the layer.
    Define what a role means roles.ROLES and compile_binding() Five human roles, one control-plane binding plus one binding per layer grant, all ALLOW. Service accounts hold no roles.
    Decide what may be discovered RoleBindingAuthorizer.visibility() dataset.discover at the resource scope, then the owning project's classification must be in the vocabulary and discoverable or cleared. Unknown codes fail closed.
    Bind an actor to its authority AccessPolicy Actor from authentication; ancestry from server records; bindings read afresh per operation; not found before forbidden.
    Turn a decision into a refusal access.check() Only an explicit ALLOW passes; the Forbidden message names capability, layer, subject, and scope level.
    Administer grants and governance records Bindings, Policies, ServiceAccounts Each guarded mutation checks the target's own scope, confirms the scope exists, and stamps the authenticated actor as provenance.
    Persist grants InMemoryRbacStore, PostgresRbacStore Validate through compile_binding before any write; duplicate grants refused; expiry filtered at read, inheritance left to the engine.
    Enforce the layer kind rule core/catalog/layers.py Catalog and Raw compose layer eligibility with Security capability decisions. Humans may write only raw and bronze, service accounts only silver and gold.

    2. Principals, scopes, bindings, and the decision procedure

    Sources: Security rules.

    Principal.identifiers is the only bridge between an actor and stored grants: sa:{subject} for a service account, user:{subject} otherwise, plus one group:{name} per group. Binding.matches() tests membership of its principal string in that set.

    Coverage is inheritance. Binding.covers() returns true for a SYSTEM binding unconditionally; otherwise it compares the binding's scope_id with the scope's ancestor field for the binding's level (organization_id, project_id, or dataset_id) or, at the binding's own level, with scope_id. A scope built without ancestry is therefore not covered by a higher binding, and a non-system binding with no scope_id covers nothing. is_expired() treats the boundary instant as expired.

    The decision procedure in decide(): collect applicable bindings (match, cover, unexpired, capability named; effect is not a filter); answer DENY if any applicable binding is a DENY, before layers are consulted; then walk DATASET, PROJECT, ORGANIZATION, SYSTEM and answer ALLOW at the first ALLOW binding whose layers admit the requested layer (None on either side lifts the restriction); otherwise DENY. The engine never loads bindings and never touches a clock except through now.

    3. Role vocabulary and compilation

    Sources: roles.py.

    A RoleDefinition is vocabulary, not enforcement. compile_binding() validates the grant through validate_binding() (role exists; principal kind is known; the kind is not service_account; the role admits the kind; the scope level is bindable) and then emits one ALLOW binding carrying the control-plane capabilities, if any, followed by one ALLOW binding per LayerGrant in definition order. Every produced binding shares principal, scope, and expiry.

    Role Bindable at Control-plane capabilities Layer grants
    reader organization, project, dataset dataset.discover data.read on every layer
    developer organization, project, dataset discover, dataset.create, dataset.update, release.create data.read every layer; data.write raw and bronze
    project_admin organization, project discover, project.update, project.policy_attach, dataset.create, dataset.update, dataset.policy_attach, release.create, rbac.binding_manage data.read every layer
    organization_admin organization discover, organization.update, organization.policy_attach, project.create, project.update, project.policy_attach, dataset.policy_attach, service_account.manage, rbac.binding_manage data.read every layer
    platform_owner system every control-plane capability including organization.create, organization.delete, user.manage data.read every layer

    All five roles admit only user principals. No role carries data.write on silver or gold, and roles_granting_write() returns nothing for those layers. service_account_bindings() synthesizes a service account's entire authority as three never-expiring organization-scope ALLOW bindings: dataset create, update, and discover; data.read on silver and gold; data.write on silver and gold. That authority is a property of the principal kind and is never stored as a row.

    CAPABILITIES holds the seventeen known capability codes. LAYER_SCOPED_CAPABILITIES names the two that carry a layers restriction; consumers of the role_capabilities table need it to tell a control-plane row from a layer row, because layers = NULL already means every layer.

    4. Classification-aware discovery

    Sources: Security rules.

    visibility() is the only producer of a Visibility. unrestricted is true only when dataset.discover is allowed at SYSTEM scope. project_ids is visible_project_ids(): the project's scope must decide dataset.discover ALLOW, its classification code must be in the vocabulary, and the level must be discoverable or cleared. Clearance comes from any unexpired ALLOW binding covering the scope whose maximum_classification ranks at or above the project's, regardless of that binding's capabilities. organization_ids holds each ORGANIZATION binding's scope whose own organization scope also decides dataset.discover ALLOW; membership there does not admit the organization's projects. dataset_ids evaluates each supplied dataset at its own scope with full ancestry and its owning project's classification; a dataset whose project is not in projects is skipped.

    The vocabulary is closed and configured per deployment (section 10). A project with an unknown code is never visible. Dataset-scoped discovery never widens to the project or sibling datasets.

    5. From authenticated actor to decision

    Sources: public Security exports, access implementation, scopes, Security facts, authenticated principal.

    as_rbac_principal() keeps only subject, groups, and kind. The API-key restrictions on security.Principal (scopes, project_id) and the authentication method are dropped and never influence a decision.

    bindings_for_principal() chooses by kind: humans and their groups resolve through stored bindings; a service account gets service_account_bindings() synthesized from its stored account, or no bindings at all if the account is missing or disabled. Both branches memoize in the caller's BindingCacheMap, keyed by identifier set. AccessPolicy passes a fresh empty cache on every call, so a core operation always reads current authority; the API's request-scoped cache (section 10) is the only place bindings are reused.

    check() is the one place a Decision becomes an error: anything but ALLOW raises Forbidden naming capability, layer, subject, and scope level.

    Not found before forbidden. The scope functions read the addressed resource through the caller's Visibility before any binding is consulted, so an absent or undiscoverable id fails as not found. Metastore's SecurityFacts.resource_scope() projects dataset ancestry after reading the target with caller visibility and its parent with Visibility.ALL. Security receives the complete Scope, never a Catalog entity. require_scope_exists() serves the governance workflows: it rejects an inconsistent scope/id pair as a caller bug (ValueError) and confirms a consistent one exists using unrestricted visibility, since the caller's own authorization has already been checked.

    6. Core consumers of AccessPolicy and capability enforcement

    Sources: Catalog creation, Catalog collections, Raw releases, Raw ingestion, Raw revision reads, Security identity.

    Every core entry class receives an AccessPolicy already bound to the authenticated actor. Operations call require() for the capability at the target's scope, visibility() for discovery-filtered reads, require_claim() to tie a retry identity to the same actor, and actor.subject as provenance in place of any caller-supplied label. DatasetCollection.layers() is the one consumer that reads bindings() and calls decide() directly, to report the caller's read and write decision for each of the four layers.

    Capability Enforced where Status
    organization.create CatalogCreation and the system guard Enforced at SYSTEM
    organization.update, organization.policy_attach _Collection.describe, Policies.attach_policy, organization guards Enforced
    organization.delete nowhere Vocabulary only; no delete workflow or route exists
    project.create, project.update, project.policy_attach CatalogCreation, _Collection.describe, Policies, ingest overseer paths, project guards Enforced
    dataset.create, dataset.update, dataset.policy_attach CatalogCreation, _Collection.describe, Policies, dataset guards Enforced
    dataset.discover RoleBindingAuthorizer.visibility() and every visibility-filtered read Enforced as discovery, not as a route guard
    release.create Releases.create_release and the dataset guard Enforced
    rbac.binding_manage Bindings and the binding routes at every scope level Enforced
    service_account.manage ServiceAccounts, IdentityService, organization guard Enforced
    user.manage IdentityService and the users routes Enforced at SYSTEM
    data.write RawIngestionService and the raw-write guards, layer raw only Enforced for raw; no bronze, silver, or gold write workflow exists
    data.read RevisionReadService, the revision download guard, layer raw only Enforced for raw payload; other layers reported by layers() only

    7. The layer kind rule at the RBAC seam

    Sources: Catalog layers.

    ensure_layer_writable() is the kind half of the write rule, checked before and independently of bindings: a service account may write silver and gold; any other kind may write only layers marked principal_writable (raw and bronze). A mis-seeded binding therefore cannot let a human commit to silver or gold, and the binding side agrees, since no role carries those writes. required_capability() returns the (data.read or data.write, layer code) pair in the order decide() takes them; the layer is never baked into a capability name. The catalog atlas section 8 covers LayerSpec in full.

    8. Governance administration

    Sources: bindings, policies, service accounts, Security ports, Security values, identity.

    Guarded-mutation rules, as implemented:

    • Bindings.grant_role() and bindings_at() require rbac.binding_manage at the addressed scope, then confirm the scope exists. revoke_role() and get_role_binding() read the binding first and check the capability at the binding's own scope, not the caller's intended one. Listing is exact-scope and includes expired grants. Grants of any sa: principal are refused by validate_binding() inside the store.
    • Policies.create_policy() and list_policies() are open to any authenticated actor, since defining a policy grants nothing. attach_policy() requires {scope}.policy_attach at the target scope, derived from the scope type's lowercase name; there is no SYSTEM attachment. spec and policy_type are stored verbatim. Nothing in the inspected source reads attachments back to enforce retention, quota, classification defaults, or schema composition.
    • ServiceAccounts requires service_account.manage on the owning organization for every operation; read and disable resolve the account first to learn its organization. Creation validates name as a slug and derives the immutable subject {organization slug}/{name}. Disabling is idempotent and does not revoke keys; IdentityService.disable_service_account() layers key revocation on top, skipping it when the account was already disabled earlier.
    • Workflows accept no caller created_by or attached_by argument. They pass the authenticated actor's subject to persistence, whose attribution parameters remain.

    9. Persistence adapters and conformance

    Sources: Metastore RBAC, hierarchy, queries, Security fact projections.

    Both stores validate a grant with compile_binding() before anything is written, deriving the principal kind from the identifier prefix (sa: is a service account). The in-memory store keeps the compiled bindings per binding id so bindings_for() is a lookup and a revoke drops exactly its own bindings. The PostgreSQL store reconstructs bindings by joining role_bindings to role_capabilities: one binding for the control-plane rows plus one per data.read/data.write row with that row's layers, filtering expired rows against the database clock and reading effect from the row, so a DENY row written outside the API is reproduced faithfully. Duplicate grants, duplicate service-account names, and repeat attachments surface as the same domain errors from both stores. The role_bindings_guard and service_accounts_kind_guard triggers repeat the validation for rows written outside the store.

    Visibility reaches SQL through _visibility_parameters() in queries.py: the unrestricted flag and the three id lists are bound as parameters of every trusted read and browse, so admission happens before pagination rather than as a post-filter.

    10. API wiring: guards, request cache, and construction

    Sources: authorization/guards.py, authorization/decisions.py, dependencies.py, app.py, settings.py, endpoints/roles.py.

    The route guards are closures over a capability. require_system() checks at SYSTEM scope; the resource guards resolve the path identifier through the caller's CurrentVisibility first, so an absent or undiscoverable id is not found before any binding is read, then check() the capability at the resolved scope. The ingest guards add ownership: an overseer is the session's creator or a holder of project.update; driving a session or an upload is the owner alone, with the raw-write binding re-checked on every call. The proof dataclasses carry the early guard result. Actor-bound Raw operations still independently re-resolve current facts and enforce their authorization; guard proofs do not replace that check.

    request_binding_cache() mints one BindingCacheMap per request through FastAPI's dependency cache; current_visibility() computes the caller's Visibility once per request. Neither survives the request. The core operations constructed by dependencies.py receive an AccessPolicy built from the same runtime, and that policy uses a fresh cache on each call. The RoleBindingAuthorizer is built once per process lifespan from ApiSettings.classification_vocabulary, whose validator refuses duplicate codes, duplicate orders, and an empty vocabulary. The roles endpoint lists ROLES directly; the API's RoleError handler renders the three role errors as 422 problems.

    11. Error hierarchy

    Sources: Security roles, Security errors, Foundation errors, Catalog layers.

    RoleError is a separate, framework-free tree whose subclasses fix code as a class variable; the API maps it to 422. DomainError carries the transport contract (code, status_code, as_problem()) and refuses direct instantiation. Forbidden is always a 403: the credential was fine, the authority was not. ResourceNotFound is what the scope functions raise for an undiscoverable id, which is how not found precedes forbidden. The 409 failures are the uniqueness rules of the governance stores. UsernameTaken and PrincipalKindMismatch belong to identity administration but share the same subject namespace that service-account subjects occupy.

    12. Designed or declared, not enforced

    Cross-checked against rbac.html and the inspected source.

    • Classification clearance is engine-only. Binding.maximum_classification is read by discovery, but no production path sets it: compile_binding() never populates it, the role_bindings table stores no conditions, and bindings_for() does not read any. In practice only classifications configured discoverable: true are ever visible to anyone without unrestricted discovery.
    • DENY bindings cannot be created through the API. Both stores insert ALLOW. The engine and PostgresRbacStore.bindings_for() honor a DENY row, but only one written outside the store.
    • organization.delete is in the vocabulary and on platform_owner; no workflow, route, or guard checks it.
    • Bronze, silver, and gold writes have no workflow. data.write is enforced only for raw ingest; data.read only for raw revision downloads and the per-layer report in DatasetCollection.layers().
    • Raw payload read is not a stricter capability. reader holds data.read on every layer including raw payload, as the design notes.
    • API-key scopes and project restriction on security.Principal are dropped by as_rbac_principal(); the RBAC tier does not narrow a key below its owner.
    • Policy attachments are stored, not interpreted. No reader composes effective policy, retention, quota, or schema requirements from them.
    • P3 integrity authority (integrity.read, integrity.maintain) is absent from CAPABILITIES and from every role; the catalog atlas notes the core/integrity subsystem separately.
    • Group membership comes only from the authenticated principal's groups; there is no group store in Security.

    Source and behavioral cross-checks

    The implementation snapshot was traced through constructors, fields, inheritance, protocol declarations, and wiring. Useful behavioral entry points are:

    • Role model tests and visibility tests: compilation, invariants on silver/gold writes, discovery and clearance.
    • Authorization decision tests, guard tests, and credential tests: the request cache, not found before forbidden, ownership, and layer rules.
    • Binding route tests, policy route tests, service-account route tests, role route tests, and RBAC route tests: governance workflows through the API.
    • RBAC store contracts, repository RBAC tests, and PostgreSQL conflict tests: adapter conformance and uniqueness errors.
    • Layer tests: the kind half of the write rule.

    This document describes inspected implementation; it does not claim that the application test suites were rerun to create a diagram.
